prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Predicting human trajectories is a cornerstone of safe autonomous vehicle operation. However, current data-driven models are brittle; they lack robustness against noisy inputs, arising either from upstream perception errors (imperfect tracking/detection) or adversarial attacks. Existing defenses are largely heuristic, offering empirical improvements but failing to provide mathematical guarantees of stability. There is currently no framework that certifies that a trajectory prediction model’s output will remain within a safe, bounded region given a specific magnitude of input perturbation.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can achieve **certified robustness** in trajectory prediction by adapting **Randomized Smoothing**—a technique traditionally used for image classification—to the domain of time-series regression.

Our central intuition is that by deliberately adding noise to inputs and aggregating the model's responses, we can statistically bound the variance of the output. Furthermore, we posit that the inherent accuracy trade-off caused by smoothing can be mitigated by introducing a **generative diffusion denoiser**. This denoiser will project noisy inputs back onto the manifold of realistic human motion before prediction, allowing us to tighten the certified bounds without sacrificing the accuracy of the trajectory forecast.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a modular pipeline designed to wrap around any standard trajectory prediction backbone to provide guaranteed output bounds.

1.  **Randomized Input Perturbation:**
    We will create a stochastic ensemble of observations by injecting controlled Gaussian noise into the input trajectory history. This serves as the foundation for the randomized smoothing certification process.

2.  **Diffusion-Based Denoising (The Pre-processor):**
    To prevent the injected noise from degrading the prediction quality, we will insert a diffusion model as a pre-processing module.
    *   *Function:* This module will be trained to act as an unconditional denoiser tailored specifically for trajectory data.
    *   *Logic:* It will take the perturbed inputs and "purify" them, recovering the underlying structure of human motion before passing the data to the prediction model. This ensures the predictor operates on data resembling its training distribution.

3.  **Aggregation Strategy for Regression:**
    Unlike classification (which uses majority voting), trajectory prediction is a regression task. We will investigate and implement aggregation operators suitable for continuous data:
    *   *Mean vs. Median Smoothing:* We will explore using dimension-wise median aggregation, as it is theoretically more robust to outliers in the predicted coordinates than the mean.

4.  **Adaptive Clamping for Unbounded Outputs:**
    Trajectory coordinates are theoretically unbounded, which complicates certification. We will implement an adaptive clamping strategy that derives maximum logical ranges from the training data distribution, enforcing a validity window for the bounds computation.

5.  **Handling Multi-Modality:**
    Since human motion is stochastic and multi-modal (multiple plausible futures), we will restructure the certification process to handle multiple output streams. We propose to certify the bounds for *all* generated modes simultaneously, ensuring that every plausible future trajectory is accompanied by a safety guarantee.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **First Certified Robustness for Trajectories:** We aim to establish the first framework capable of providing mathematical guarantees (certified bounds) for human trajectory prediction, moving beyond empirical defenses.
2.  **Robustness-Accuracy Balance:** By integrating a diffusion denoiser, we expect to solve the "curse of smoothing," delivering tight safety bounds while maintaining high prediction accuracy.
3.  **Reliability Metrics:** We intend to define new evaluation metrics (e.g., Certified Displacement Error) that assess models not just on how close they are to the ground truth, but on the worst-case performance under guaranteed noise bounds.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of certified trajectory prediction methods, focusing on robustness against noise and adversarial attacks.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **ETH** and **UCY**: Crowd datasets containing human position annotations.
    *   **WildTrack**: Dense unscripted pedestrian detection dataset.
    *   **Benchmark:** We utilized the **Trajnet++** benchmark for fixed data splits and unified pre-processing.
    *   **Sequence Lengths:** Input observation length ($T_{obs}$) was set to 9 timesteps. Prediction output length ($T_{pred}$) was set to 12 timesteps.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **ADE / FDE:** Average Displacement Error and Final Displacement Error (standard accuracy metrics).
    *   **ABD / FBD:** Average Bound half-Diameter and Final Bound half-Diameter (measures the tightness of the certified bound; FBD measures the distance at the final timestep).
    *   **Certified-ADE / Certified-FDE:** Measures the highest ADE/FDE occurring given noisy inputs (distance of the farthest point inside the bounds to the ground truth).
    *   **Certified-Col (Certified Collision Rate):** Percentage of examples where at least one neighboring agent lies within the calculated certified bounds of the predicted trajectory.
    *   **Downstream Metrics:** Reward (accumulated) and Collision Rate (%) for the robot navigation task.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Social-Force:** Rule-based trajectory predictor.
    *   **D-Pool (Directional-Pooling):** Learning-based state-of-the-art predictor.
    *   **AutoBot:** Learning-based state-of-the-art predictor.
    *   **Eq-Motion:** Learning-based state-of-the-art predictor.
    *   **Smoothed Variants:** We created smoothed versions of all the above (Smoothed Social-Force, Smoothed D-Pool, Smoothed AutoBot, Smoothed EqMotion).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Certification Method:** Randomized Smoothing (evaluating both Mean and Median aggregation).
    *   **Monte-Carlo Samples ($n$):** Set to 100.
    *   **Certification Radius ($R$):** Set to 0.1.
    *   **Noise Hyperparameter ($\sigma$):** Range evaluated from 0.08 to 0.4.
    *   **Denoiser:** An unconditional diffusion-based denoiser (simple autoencoder structure) trained to reverse the Gaussian noise process.
    *   **Hardware:** Experiments were run on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090.
    *   **Inference Time:** 0.07 seconds for the original EqMotion; 0.1 seconds for Smoothed EqMotion ($n=100$).
    *   **Downstream Simulation:** Crowd navigation simulator generating 5,000 simulation episodes; imitation model trained for 200 epochs.

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Table 1: Comparison of performance in terms of certified and non-certified metrics across different models**
| Model | FDE (m) | Certified-FDE (m) | Col (%) | Certified-Col (%) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Social-Force | 1.25 | N/A | 7.4 | N/A |
| Smoothed Social-Force | 1.26 | 2.27 | 8.0 | 46 |
| D-Pool | 1.14 | N/A | 9.4 | N/A |
| Smoothed D-Pool | 1.23 | 2.0 | 9.0 | 49 |
| AutoBot | 1.14 | N/A | 8.8 | N/A |
| Smoothed AutoBot | 1.17 | 2.05 | 9.3 | 53 |
| EqMotion | 1.12 | N/A | 10.1 | N/A |
| Smoothed EqMotion | 1.14 | 2.07 | 10.6 | 57 |

**Table 2: Performance comparison of different denoisers (remaining noise magnitude reported)**
| Model | Noise = 0.08 | Noise = 0.24 | Noise = 0.40 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| No denoiser | 0.08 | 0.24 | 0.40 |
| Polynomial | 0.08 | 0.22 | 0.36 |
| Moving Average | 0.07 | 0.18 | 0.29 |
| Wiener Filter | 0.06 | 0.16 | 0.26 |
| Diffusion Denoiser (ours) | 0.06 | 0.14 | 0.24 |

**Table 3: Comparison of FBD of the smoothed predictor with and without the denoiser across different FDE values**
| Model | FDE = 1.2 | FDE = 1.3 | FDE = 1.4 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| W/o denoiser | 1.20 | 0.96 | 0.80 |
| W/ denoiser | 0.78 | 0.65 | 0.57 |

**Table 4: Comparison of single- vs. multi-modal settings for Smoothed EqMotion**
| Model | FDE (m) | FBD (m) | Certified-FDE (m) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Single-modal | 1.13 | 0.99 | 2.07 |
| Multi-modal | 0.39 | 0.64 | 1.38 |

**Table 5: Comparison of certified bounds in single- vs. multi-agent settings at similar FDE values**
| Model | FDE (m) | FBD (m) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Single-agent | 1.13 | 0.99 |
| Multi-agent | 1.13 | 1.21 |

**Table 6: Quantitative results of crowd robot navigation with different prediction methods**
| Method | Noise size | Reward ↑ | Collision (%) ↓ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Original | 0 | 0.272 | 13.1 |
| Original | 0.2 | 0.230 | 21.0 |
| Robust | 0.2 | 0.263 | 15.1 |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Model Accuracy vs. Robustness Trade-off**
*   We observed a trade-off between accuracy and certified bounds: as the hyperparameter $\sigma$ increased, the certified bounds tightened (lower FBD) while the accuracy decreased (higher FDE).
*   Median aggregation produced considerably smaller bounds compared to mean aggregation, indicating better alignment with the trajectory prediction task.
*   Smoothed D-Pool exhibited smaller bounds for FDE values below 1.25 compared to Smoothed EqMotion and Smoothed AutoBot.
*   Smoothed Social-Force demonstrated the largest bounds, attributed to its high sensitivity to input perturbations.
*   We found that the most accurate models (based on standard FDE) were not necessarily the most robust (based on Certified-FDE). For example, while EqMotion had the lowest FDE, Smoothed D-Pool achieved a lower Certified-FDE.

**Robustness Against Attacks and Noise**
*   Original predictors produced unbounded predictions when subjected to noisy inputs, whereas our certified predictor provided bounds that contained the outputs.
*   Under PGD adversarial attacks, original models showed large deviations (greater than 2 meters) from their original predictions. In contrast, the smoothed predictor's outputs consistently remained within the certified bounds under the same attacks.
*   When using imperfect observation trajectories derived from an off-the-shelf detection and tracking system (on nuScenes data), the original model's predictions deviated significantly from those based on ground-truth observations. The smoothed predictor maintained predictions within certified bounds for these imperfect inputs.

**Ablation and Component Analysis**
*   **Denoiser Effectiveness:** The proposed diffusion denoiser outperformed statistical approaches (Wiener filter, Moving Average, Polynomial fitting) in reducing noise magnitude across all tested noise levels (0.08, 0.24, 0.40).
*   **Impact on Bounds:** Integrating the denoiser significantly tightened the certified bounds. For a fixed FDE of 1.2, the FBD was reduced from 1.20 (without denoiser) to 0.78 (with denoiser).
*   **Multi-modality:** The multi-modal smoothed model (using $k=20$ modes) achieved better accuracy (lower FDE) and tighter bounds (lower FBD) compared to the single-modal counterpart, as different modes captured specific behaviors.
*   **Multi-agent:** When extending certification to multi-agent settings (perturbing all agents), the certified bounds were larger than in single-agent settings for similar FDE values, due to interdependencies between agents.

**Downstream Application**
*   In the crowd robot navigation task, the learned policy proved sensitive to input noise, with collision rates rising from 13.1% (clean) to 21.0% (noisy).
*   Incorporating the diffusion denoiser improved the accumulated reward and reduced the collision rate to 15.1% in the presence of noise.

**Computational Cost**
*   The evaluation time for predicting a trajectory on an RTX 3090 increased from 0.07 seconds (original EqMotion) to 0.1 seconds (Smoothed EqMotion with $n=100$), representing a roughly 42% increase, which remains feasible for real-time applications.

[AVAILABLE FIGURES]
### AVAILABLE FIGURES LIST

The red trajectories depict clean observations and the corresponding predictions, while the gray trajectories show noisy observations along with their resulting predictions. In contrast, the bottom part demonstrates the outputs of our trajectory predictor with guaranteed robustness. The model provides certified bounds (blue boxes) on the predicted outputs, ensuring that outputs remain within guaranteed regions despite input noise.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 2:
  - Filename: figure_3.png
  - Caption: Figure 3. FDE against FBD for median aggregation on the left and mean aggregation on the right. The results are for different smoothed predictors with two aggregation functions and equally spaced σ within [0.08, 0.4]. The bottom left indicates the best performance. The figures show a trade-off between accuracy (represented in FDE) and robustness (represented as FBD). They also provide a comparison between models’ guaranteed robustness.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 3:
  - Filename: figure_4.png
  - Caption: Figure 4. Comparing the performance of the original (on the left) and the smoothed predictor (on the right). The original predictor’s outputs change drastically with adversarial and imperfect inputs. In contrast, the smoothed predictor consistently predicts within the bounds, demonstrating higher reliability. For easier comparison, the final predicted points of the original predictor for the adversarial and imperfect observations are marked on the right figure with gray and blue stars, respectively.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 4:
  - Filename: figure_2.png
  - Caption: Figure 2. An outline of the proposed smoothed trajectory predictor: n different randomized input observations Xi are created by adding perturbation ϵ to the input X . The denoiser h processes these samples Xi, which are then fed into the trajectory predictor g to make the outputs Y i. Applying an aggregation function A (median or mean) on Y i, the final smoothed prediction Y is derived.
--------------------------------------------------

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Example Code for Tables

  \centering
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
    \toprule
    Method & Frobnability \\
    \midrule
    Theirs & Frumpy \\

    Ours & Makes one's heart Frob\\

  \end{tabular}

  \label{tab:example}
\end{table}
```

   It is set in Roman so that mathematics (always set in Roman: $B \sin A = A \sin B$) may be included without an ugly clash.}
   \label{fig:onecol}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure*}

    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{An example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-a}
  \end{subfigure}
  \hfill
  \begin{subfigure}{0.28\linewidth}
    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{Another example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-b}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Example of a short caption, which should be centered.}
  \label{fig:short}
\end{figure*}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-11.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---
### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Human trajectory prediction is a cornerstone of safe autonomous vehicle operation, aiming to forecast future positions of pedestrians based on past observations. However, current data-driven approaches—typically deep neural networks—operate as "black boxes" and lack guaranteed robustness. They are highly susceptible to input noise, whether arising from imperfect upstream perception modules (detection and tracking errors) or malicious adversarial attacks. Existing defense mechanisms in this domain are primarily heuristic; while they may improve empirical robustness against specific attacks, they fail to provide theoretical guarantees. There is currently no framework that certifies that a trajectory predictor's output will remain within a bounded region given a bounded perturbation in the input. This lack of certifiability renders current predictors unreliable for safety-critical applications where worst-case behavior must be bounded.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that we can achieve **guaranteed robustness** for human trajectory prediction by adapting **Randomized Smoothing**—a certification technique traditionally used for classification—to the multi-output, time-series regression domain of trajectory forecasting.

By adding controlled Gaussian noise to the input and aggregating the resulting stochastic predictions, we can statistically derive a "smoothed" predictor. We postulate that this smoothed predictor will possess certified bounds: for any input perturbation within a defined $\ell_2$ radius, the output trajectory will provably remain within a calculated geometric envelope. Furthermore, to mitigate the accuracy degradation typically associated with smoothing, we propose integrating an **unconditional diffusion-based denoiser** as a pre-processor. We hypothesize that this denoiser will recover the underlying signal from the randomized inputs before they reach the predictor, thereby tightening the certified bounds without retraining the core prediction model.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework to transform any standard trajectory predictor into a robust, certified predictor. Our methodology consists of four key components: mathematical formulation of the smoothing operations (Mean and Median), a diffusion-based denoising module, strategies for handling unbounded/multi-modal outputs, and the definition of certified performance metrics.

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of the Task

We define the trajectory prediction task as a regression problem mapping an observed sequence to a future sequence. Let the position of an agent at timestep $t$ be $(x_t, y_t)$. Given an observation sequence $X = (x_{-T_{\mathrm{obs}}+1}, y_{-T_{\mathrm{obs}}+1}, \dots, x_0, y_0) \in \mathbb{R}^{2T_{\mathrm{obs}}}$, the base predictor $g$ outputs a prediction $Y = g(X) = (x_1, y_1, \dots, x_{T_{\mathrm{pred}}}, y_{T_{\mathrm{pred}}}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2T_{\mathrm{pred}}}$.

We aim to certify a smoothed function $\tilde{f}$ derived from $g$, such that for an input $X$ and a perturbation $r$ where $\|r\|_2 < R$ (the certification radius), the output $\tilde{f}(X+r)$ is bounded.

### 2. Randomized Smoothing Strategies

We will investigate two aggregation operators, $\mathcal{A}$, to construct the smoothed function $\tilde{f}(X) = \mathcal{A}(g(X + \epsilon))$, where $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$.

**A. Mean Smoothing with Adaptive Clamping**
Mean smoothing computes the expected value: $\tilde{f}(X) = \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}[g(X+\epsilon)]$.
Standard mean smoothing requires the output function to be bounded within $[l, u]$. Since trajectory coordinates are unbounded, we will implement **Adaptive Clamping**. We will estimate coordinate-wise bounds $l_j = \min_X f_j(X)$ and $u_j = \max_X f_j(X)$ from the training set. We will then clamp the predictor's output using the operator $\min(u_j, \max(l_j, \cdot))$.
The certified bounds for the smoothed output will be:
$$ l + (u - l) \cdot \Phi \left( \frac{\eta(X) - R}{\sigma} \right) \leq \tilde{f}(X + r) \leq l + (u - l) \cdot \Phi \left( \frac{\eta(X) + R}{\sigma} \right) $$
where $\eta(X) = \sigma \cdot \Phi^{-1} \left( \frac{\tilde{f}(X) - l}{u - l} \right)$ and $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard Gaussian.

**B. Median Smoothing**
To avoid the artificial constraints of clamping, we will also implement median smoothing, which is naturally suited for regression. We define the smoothed function as the coordinate-wise median: $\tilde{f}(X) = q_{0.5}(X)$, where $q_p(X)$ is the $p$-th quantile of the distribution of $g(X+\epsilon)$.
The certified lower and upper bounds (LB and UB) will be derived as:
$$ q_{\Phi(-R/\sigma)}(X) \leq \tilde{f}(X+r) \leq q_{\Phi(R/\sigma)}(X) $$
This method does not require pre-computed output ranges.

### 3. Diffusion-Based Trajectory Denoiser

To improve the trade-off between robustness (tight bounds) and accuracy, we will prepend a denoiser $h$ to the predictor, such that the composite model is $f(X) = g(h(X))$.
We will design $h$ as a **Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM)** tailored for trajectory data.
*   **Architecture:** An unconditional autoencoder trained to reconstruct clean trajectories from noisy versions.
*   **Training:** We will add Gaussian noise progressively to training trajectories and train the model to reverse this process.
*   **Inference:** For every Monte-Carlo sample $X^i = X + \epsilon$, the denoiser will map $X^i$ to a projected "clean" manifold state before it is processed by $g$.

### 4. Handling Multi-Modality

Trajectory prediction is inherently multi-modal, often outputting $k$ plausible futures. We will adapt the certification process to handle dimensions $\mathbb{R}^{2T_{\mathrm{obs}}} \to \mathbb{R}^{k \times 2T_{\mathrm{pred}}}$.
We will certify all $k$ modes independently. During evaluation, we will select the "best" mode based on the minimum Certified-FDE (defined below). This approach acknowledges that distinct modes represent distinct semantic behaviors, and robustness should be guaranteed per behavior.

### 5. Certified Performance Metrics

Standard metrics (ADE/FDE) cannot measure guaranteed robustness. We will define and implement the following certified metrics:

*   **Final Bound half-Diameter (FBD):** Measures the tightness of the guarantee at the final timestep.
    $$ \mathrm{FBD} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{ (\mathrm{UB}_{2T_{\mathrm{pred}}-1} - \mathrm{LB}_{2T_{\mathrm{pred}}-1})^2 + (\mathrm{UB}_{2T_{\mathrm{pred}}} - \mathrm{LB}_{2T_{\mathrm{pred}}})^2 } $$
*   **Certified-ADE/FDE:** The worst-case displacement error within the certified bounds. This measures the distance from the ground truth to the *farthest* point inside the certified region.
*   **Certified Collision Rate:** The percentage of scenarios where *any* point within the predicted certified bounds collides with a neighbor's ground-truth trajectory.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **First Certified Framework:** We will establish the first certification method for human trajectory prediction, shifting the paradigm from empirical to guaranteed robustness.
2.  **Adapted Smoothing Techniques:** We will provide the formulation for applying Mean and Median randomized smoothing to unbounded, multi-modal time-series data.
3.  **Diffusion Integration:** We expect to demonstrate that an unconditional diffusion denoiser can effectively project perturbed inputs back to the data manifold, significantly tightening certified bounds compared to raw smoothing.
4.  **Novel Metrics:** We will establish a new standard for evaluating safety in trajectory prediction through certified metrics (Certified-FDE, FBD) that account for worst-case input noise.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
